subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which is an example of a 'push' factor for migration?
options: Conflict or persecution in the home country
A safe and peaceful environment in the destination
questions.explain: Push factors drive people away from their home area; conflict and persecution are common push factors.

questions.q: Besides migration, what is the other main cause of urban population growth?
options: Natural increase, where births exceed deaths
questions.explain: Cities often have a young population, so a high birth rate combined with a lower death rate causes natural increase.

questions.q: A country with an ageing population is likely to experience:
options: A rising dependency ratio and higher pension costs
questions.explain: An ageing population means more elderly dependants, raising the dependency ratio and increasing pension and healthcare costs.

questions.q: In Stage 4 of the Demographic Transition Model, population is typically:
options: High and stable with low birth and death rates
questions.explain: In Stage 4 both birth and death rates are low, so the population is high and roughly stable.

questions.q: The dependency ratio compares:
options: The non-working (young and old) population to the working-age population
questions.explain: The dependency ratio measures how many dependants (young and elderly) rely on each person of working age.

questions.q: Which of these is a 'push' factor encouraging rural-to-urban migration?
options: Entertainment and shops in the city
Lack of services and poverty in the countryside
Good schools and hospitals in the city
questions.explain: Push factors drive people away from an area, such as rural poverty, drought and a lack of services.

questions.q: Which factor encourages a high population density?
options: Dense tropical rainforest with poor soils
A flat, fertile area with a temperate climate
questions.explain: Flat fertile land with a moderate climate supports farming and settlement, leading to higher population densities.

questions.q: A pro-natalist population policy aims to:
options: Encourage couples to have more children
questions.explain: Pro-natalist policies use incentives such as benefits and childcare to raise birth rates in countries with ageing populations.

questions.q: A negative impact of migration on the SOURCE (origin) country is often:
options: A loss of working-age people and skills ('brain drain')
More money spent locally by migrants
questions.explain: When working-age and skilled people emigrate, the source country can suffer a 'brain drain' and labour shortages.

questions.q: Why is providing clean water and sanitation a major challenge in fast-growing squatter settlements?
options: Settlements grow faster than services can be built, and many are unplanned
Residents refuse to use clean water
There is too much government funding
There is no demand for water in slums
questions.explain: Unplanned settlements often grow too quickly for authorities to provide piped water and sewerage, spreading disease.

questions.q: Overpopulation occurs when:
options: The population exceeds the resources available to support it
Birth and death rates are equal
There are too few people to use resources fully
A country has lots of empty land
questions.explain: Overpopulation is when the number of people exceeds the resources and technology available to maintain a good standard of living.

questions.q: Which of these is a 'pull' factor attracting people to cities?
questions.explain: Pull factors attract people to an area, such as the prospect of jobs, schools, hospitals and a higher standard of living.

questions.q: Underpopulation occurs when:
options: Birth and death rates are equal
A country has no natural resources
There are too few people to use the resources available effectively
questions.explain: Underpopulation is when a country has more resources than its population can fully use, often limiting economic development.

questions.q: In many UK cities, old industrial dockland areas have been regenerated mainly to:
options: Create new housing, offices and leisure facilities
questions.explain: Regeneration of derelict docklands, such as in London or Liverpool, creates modern housing, business and leisure spaces.

questions.q: Which of these is a common challenge caused by rapid urban growth in LICs and NEEs?
options: Too few people to fill jobs
questions.explain: Rapid growth can overwhelm services such as water, sanitation and transport, leading to congestion and pollution.

questions.q: Which of these is a feature of a sustainable city?
options: Efficient public transport and plenty of green space
questions.explain: Sustainable cities promote public transport, recycling, green spaces and renewable energy to reduce their environmental impact.

questions.q: China's former one-child policy is an example of:
questions.explain: The one-child policy aimed to reduce births, making it an anti-natalist population policy.

questions.q: Which is an example of a 'pull' factor for migration?
options: Better job opportunities in the destination
questions.explain: Pull factors attract people to a new place; better jobs in the destination is a classic pull factor.

questions.q: Building on previously developed 'brownfield' sites within a city helps sustainability because it:
options: Reuses derelict land and protects greenfield sites
questions.explain: Brownfield development reuses abandoned urban land, reducing pressure to build on undeveloped greenfield countryside.

questions.q: On a settlement hierarchy, which has the highest order and largest range of services?
questions.explain: Cities and conurbations sit at the top of the settlement hierarchy with the largest populations and widest range of services.

questions.q: The 'site' of a settlement refers to:
options: The actual land on which it is built
Its position relative to other places
questions.explain: Site describes the physical land a settlement is built on, while situation describes its position relative to surroundings.

questions.q: Why do many people in LIC/NEE cities work in the 'informal' economy?
options: They cannot find formal, regulated jobs
The government requires it by law
It offers high wages and pensions
questions.explain: With too few formal jobs, many migrants do unregulated, low-paid informal work such as street selling to survive.
